passage:
Week one, Monday: The science fair topics went up. Anand chose water filters and told Disha it would be easy. "I'll start this weekend." He didn't. Every time he opened the notebook he pictured the judges frowning, and Disha's model from last year, and closed it again. "I work better at the end anyway," he said.
Week three, Wednesday: Four days left. Disha asked to see his plan. "Still thinking," he said, and switched the talk to cricket.
Fair day, Saturday: Anand's filter leaked on the table. The poster had spelling mistakes he would have caught with a spare hour. A judge was kind: the idea was good, the testing was thin. Walking home he told Disha, quietly, "If I'd started early and it was bad, that would really be me. This way it's just the rushing."

qa.q: What did the judge say about Anand's project?
qa.a: That the idea was good and the testing was thin.

qa.q: Why did Anand keep closing the notebook?
qa.a: Opening it made him picture frowning judges and Disha's strong model; not starting kept him from finding out he might not be good enough, which felt safer.

qa.q: What was the turning point Anand missed, and what could he try next time?
qa.a: Week one, when the dread first showed; building a rough first filter early and showing it to one person would bring feedback while there was still time to fix it.

qa.q: How might Disha see Anand's "Still thinking" in week three?
qa.a: Disha may sense he is stuck and uneasy and feel unsure whether to push or leave him be; only his confession on the way home explains what Disha couldn't see.

grounding: A teenager delays a science project to avoid being judged, which protects his self-image but leaves the project rushed.

passage: Nikita, beta, come sit. You say you'll do the history project later? Let me tell you about your Dadu at fifteen. Our headmaster announced an essay competition, and my teacher said, "Gautam, you write well, you must enter." I was so proud, and so scared. What if I wrote it and it was ordinary? Then everyone would know I wasn't special. So I didn't write. I told myself I was collecting ideas. I played carrom, I cleaned my bicycle twice. The night before, I wrote it by lantern in two hours. It won nothing. And the worst part, Nikita, was that I never learned whether I was any good, because what I handed in wasn't me really trying. So start yours ugly, today. Ugly can be fixed.

qa.q: What did Gautam's teacher say about the essay competition?
qa.a: "Gautam, you write well, you must enter."

qa.q: Why did Gautam feel both proud and scared?
qa.a: The praise made him proud but raised the stakes: an ordinary essay would prove he wasn't special, so not writing felt like protecting the teacher's good opinion.

qa.q: What choice does Dadu urge Nikita to make?
qa.a: To start the history project today, even roughly, since an ugly first draft can be fixed while a last-night rush leaves no room to improve.

qa.q: What might Nikita take from hearing Dadu admit this?
qa.a: Nikita may feel less alone with the fear of being judged, and a grandfather owning up to his own mistake makes the advice feel like help rather than a scolding.

grounding: A grandfather recalls delaying an essay at fifteen to avoid a verdict on his ability, which made the final essay worse.

passage: Sarika had three weeks to send four drawings for the district art scholarship. Her older cousin had won it once, and everyone at home said, "Your turn now." Sarika kept her sketchbook shut. "The light's bad in the evenings," she told Irawati, which was true: the power in their lane went off most nights. But she didn't draw on bright Sunday afternoons either. She sorted her pencils, watched videos of other artists and said she was waiting to feel inspired. With four days left, the power cuts got worse, and she drew by the torch on Irawati's phone, hurrying, smudging the charcoal. She sent the drawings at midnight. "At least if they reject it," she said, "it's because I rushed, not because I can't draw." Irawati didn't answer.

qa.q: How did Sarika light her drawings in the last four days?
qa.a: She drew by the torch on Irawati's phone.

qa.q: What does Sarika's final remark reveal about why she waited?
qa.a: She was afraid her best effort might not be good enough; rushing gave her something else to blame, which felt safer than risking a real verdict on her skill.

qa.q: How could Sarika have handled the power cuts and the fear?
qa.a: Using the bright Sunday afternoons for rough sketches, even imperfect ones, so the scary first step happened early and the power cuts mattered less.

qa.q: Why might Irawati stay silent after Sarika's remark?
qa.a: Irawati may see that the excuse hides fear and not know how to say so kindly at midnight, or may simply be worn out after lending the phone torch for days.

grounding: A teenager avoids starting a scholarship portfolio so that a poor result can be blamed on rushing, and the work suffers.

passage: The Class 10 science project was due in three weeks, and Kunal hadn't opened the kit. Every evening in their Bhopal flat he tidied his desk, sharpened pencils and watched videos of other students' models, each one better than anything he could picture making. His friend Samir had already built a solar oven. "You topped the mock," Samir said on the school bus. "Yours will be amazing." Kunal felt his throat tighten. If it wasn't amazing, everyone would know the topper was a fake. So he waited. Two nights before the deadline he finally started, with glue that wouldn't set and the stationery shop already closed. The model leaned sideways. "I didn't have time," he told the teacher, which was almost true.

qa.q: What had Samir already built?
qa.a: Samir had already built a solar oven.

qa.q: Why did Kunal's throat tighten when Samir said his model would be amazing?
qa.a: He feared an ordinary model would expose him as a 'fake' topper 😰, so not starting felt safer than finding out.

qa.q: What small step could Kunal have taken in the first week?
qa.a: Build one rough piece, like the base, with nobody watching and permission to be imperfect; starting early would have left time to fix it.

qa.q: How might Samir's praise look different if Samir knew what Kunal was feeling?
qa.a: Samir meant it kindly but might see it added pressure, and could offer to build side by side instead of predicting something amazing.

grounding: A teenager puts off a science project because a weak result would threaten his image as a topper, and the late work turns out worse.

passage:
"Simran, the debate video is due Monday. Have you recorded anything?"
"Not yet, Rekha Didi. I'm still researching."
"You've been researching for two weeks."
"It has to be good. Mrs Thomas said I have the best voice in class."
"So record a practice one. Just for me."
"No!" Simran pulled her knees up on the bed. "If it comes out bad, then she was wrong about me."
Rekha sat down beside her. "And if you record it Sunday night at eleven, what then?"
"Then it's bad because I rushed. That's different."
"Is it? Either way it's rushed, and you lose sleep too."
Simran picked at the bedsheet. "It's easier to blame the clock."
"I know. Record one line now. Just one. I'll make chai."

qa.q: Who said Simran has the best voice in class?
qa.a: Mrs Thomas said she has the best voice in class.

qa.q: What does 'It's easier to blame the clock' reveal about Simran's thinking?
qa.a: Simran is afraid of being judged: if the video is rushed, a poor result can be blamed on time rather than on her, so waiting protects her belief that she has the best voice.

qa.q: What choice does Rekha offer, and why might it work?
qa.a: Recording just one line right now, with chai; it is small enough to feel safe and breaks the wait before Sunday night makes the work worse.

qa.q: How does Rekha seem to see Simran's 'researching'?
qa.a: Rekha sees the fear under it and, rather than scolding, points out that rushing still gives a poor result, only with less sleep.

grounding: A teenager delays recording a debate video because a weak result would disprove her teacher's praise, and her sister points out the cost.

passage: The science exhibition at the government higher secondary school in Kottayam was on the twentieth. Elizabeth had known since the first week of the month. Her partner Suraj kept asking at the bus stand, "Did you start the water filter model?" and she kept saying, "This weekend." The truth was, every time she opened her notebook, she pictured the judges from the district office staring at a leaking bottle while everyone watched. If she didn't start, nobody could see it fail. On the eighteenth, Suraj turned up at her house with sand, charcoal and two plastic bottles. They built it on the verandah until the power cut at nine, working by torchlight. On the day, the water came out cloudy. Elizabeth stood beside it with her arms folded tight, thinking: if I'd had time, it would have been clear.

qa.q: What model were Elizabeth and Suraj supposed to build?
qa.a: A water filter model for the science exhibition.

qa.q: Why did putting off the project feel safer to Elizabeth?
qa.a: She felt afraid of being judged; if she didn't start, nobody could see the model fail, which protected her image of herself.

qa.q: What small step would help Elizabeth start earlier on the next project?
qa.a: She could build a rough test version privately in the first week, so any failure happens early and only in front of Suraj, not the judges.

qa.q: How is Suraj affected by Elizabeth's delay?
qa.a: Suraj ends up worried and rushed, bringing materials himself and working late by torchlight to save their shared project.

grounding: It shows a teenager who delayed a project to avoid a poor result revealing weakness, which protected her self-image but made the final model worse.

passage: Kwame had three weeks to write the history essay on his family's migration from Kumasi to London. Mr Emil, his teacher, had called it the essay that would decide his predicted grade. That was the problem. Every evening Kwame opened the laptop, typed a title, and then remembered how his cousin's essay had been read aloud in assembly. If he tried properly and it was only average, it would prove he wasn't clever, not really. So he cleaned his football boots. He reorganised his bookshelf. He told his mum he was "gathering sources." The night before the deadline, he wrote from ten until three, without time to call his grandfather for the stories he'd planned to use. The essay came back with a B minus and a note: "Where is your grandfather's voice?" Kwame stared at it and thought, at least I didn't really try.

qa.q: What was Kwame's history essay about?
qa.a: It was about his family's migration from Kumasi to London.

qa.q: Why does Kwame think 'at least I didn't really try' when the essay comes back?
qa.a: He was scared that a real effort ending in an average grade would prove he wasn't clever, so a rushed essay feels less painful and protects his pride, even though he's disappointed.

qa.q: What could Kwame try next time a big piece of work feels frightening?
qa.a: He could start with one small, low-stakes step early, like calling his grandfather in the first week, and show a rough draft to Mr Emil before it counts.

qa.q: How might Mr Emil see the missing grandfather voice?
qa.a: Mr Emil might be disappointed and puzzled, sensing Kwame could have done much better, without knowing the fear behind the delay.

grounding: It shows a teenager who delayed an important essay because a poor result would expose weakness, which protected his self-image but weakened the essay.

passage: The art room at Sunrise Residential School smelled of turpentine and damp paper. Every Class 11 student had a canvas for the annual exhibition, and Sangeeta ma'am pinned a schedule on the board: sketch by week one, colours by week three. Minakshi's canvas stayed blank until week four. She wasn't lazy. She had filled three sketchbooks at home. But this canvas would hang in the corridor where parents, juniors, and the principal walked past, with her name on a card beneath it. Every time she lifted the pencil, she saw someone squinting at a wobbly line. Sangeeta ma'am asked twice. "I'm still thinking about composition," Minakshi said. In the last four days she painted fast, and the sky dried in streaks she had no time to fix. At the opening she stood far from her canvas, pretending to admire someone else's.

qa.q: How many sketchbooks had Minakshi filled at home?
qa.a: She had filled three sketchbooks at home.

qa.q: What does Minakshi standing far from her canvas suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt embarrassed and exposed, wanting distance from a painting she feared would be judged, the same fear that kept the canvas blank.

qa.q: How could Sangeeta ma'am support a student like Minakshi earlier?
qa.a: She could ask to see small, private steps, like a rough sketch in her notebook, and remind her that early drafts are meant to be imperfect.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta ma'am read Minakshi's 'still thinking about composition' answer?
qa.a: Sangeeta ma'am might see it as careful planning at first, then feel concerned as the weeks pass without any work on the canvas.

grounding: It shows a teenager who delayed a public art project because a weak result would reveal weakness, which protected her self-image but made the painting worse.

passage:
Subject: Science exhibition project

Dear Jomon Sir,

I'm sorry the project isn't ready. I know you asked for the first draft on Monday and it's now Thursday.

I want to be honest, because you've been kind to me.

I haven't been lazy. I've opened the file almost every evening. But each time, I think: what if my water-filter model doesn't work? What if everyone sees it and thinks I'm not as good as they thought? So I close it and do something else, and tell myself I'll start fresh tomorrow.

Now I have less time than ever, and the model will probably be worse than if I'd started last week. I can see that.

Could I show you what I have tomorrow, even if it's rough? I think it would help to have someone look at it early.

Gargi

qa.q: What is Gargi's science exhibition project?
qa.a: Gargi's project is a water-filter model.

qa.q: Why does Gargi keep closing the file?
qa.a: Gargi feels anxious that a model that fails would reveal weakness, so putting it off protects Gargi's self-image.

qa.q: What step does Gargi propose, and why might it help?
qa.a: Showing Jomon Sir the rough work tomorrow; early feedback makes the task less scary and gives time to fix it.

qa.q: How might Jomon Sir feel reading this email?
qa.a: Jomon Sir might feel concerned but touched by the honesty, and glad to help early.

grounding: The email shows a teenager delaying a project because a poor result might reveal weakness, making the eventual work worse.

passage:
You're asking why I handed in the history project two days late, Santosh? Okay. Honestly.
I'm Vikas. Everyone thinks I'm the clever one. Teachers say it. My parents say it. So when Ma'am gave us the project on the freedom movement, I thought: this has to be brilliant. If it isn't, everyone will know I'm not actually that clever.
So I didn't start. Every evening I'd sit down, look at the empty chart paper, and feel sick. I'd reorganise my pens, check my phone, think “tomorrow.”
Then it was the night before. I rushed. The chart was messy, the timeline had a mistake, and I stayed up till 2.
I got a B minus. The funny thing is, if I'd started two weeks earlier, it would've been fine. I avoided looking weak, and ended up looking worse.

qa.q: What grade did Vikas get for the history project?
qa.a: Vikas got a B minus.

qa.q: Why did Vikas feel sick looking at the empty chart paper?
qa.a: Vikas felt anxious that a poor project would show Vikas isn't actually clever, so starting felt threatening.

qa.q: What could Vikas try for the next project?
qa.a: Start early with a rough draft that doesn't need to be brilliant, and show it to someone for feedback.

qa.q: How might Santosh see Vikas as “the clever one” who submitted late?
qa.a: Santosh might feel surprised, not realising how much pressure the label put on Vikas.

grounding: The monologue shows a teenager delaying a project because a poor result would reveal weakness, which makes the final work worse.

passage:
Week 1: Sunaina's art teacher assigned a portfolio for the district competition. Sunaina, fifteen, loved drawing, but every time she sat down she imagined the judges saying, “Ordinary.” She sharpened pencils and closed the sketchbook.
Week 3: Her friend Alka asked how it was going. “Haven't started. I want it to be perfect.” Alka frowned. “You've got one week.” Sunaina laughed it off, but her stomach twisted.
Week 4: The night before submission, Sunaina drew four pieces in a panic. The lines were shaky. One had a smudge she couldn't fix.
When the results came, her work wasn't selected. The judge's note said, “Talented, but rushed.”
Sunaina read it twice. Rushed. Not ordinary. She'd protected herself from “ordinary” and got “rushed” instead.

qa.q: What did the judge's note say?
qa.a: It said, “Talented, but rushed.”

qa.q: Why did Sunaina close the sketchbook in week 1?
qa.a: She felt afraid the judges would call her work ordinary, so avoiding it protected her self-image.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could she try next time?
qa.a: Delay forced a rushed night of drawing; starting early with rough sketches she can improve would give her work its real chance.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt hearing “Haven't started” in week 3?
qa.a: Alka probably felt worried and a bit frustrated, seeing a friend running out of time.

grounding: The three beats show a teenager delaying a portfolio because a poor result might reveal weakness, and the eventual rushed work being worse.

passage:
"Gopika, you've been 'about to start' that project for ten days. Let me tell you about your Irawati Ajji at sixteen.
We had a science exhibition. Each of us had to build a working model. I wanted to make a water filter, and I knew it would be judged in front of the whole school, even the parents.
And I was frightened. What if it leaked? What if everyone saw I wasn't clever? So I didn't start. Each evening I told my mother, 'Tomorrow.' Somehow, not starting felt safer than starting badly.
Three days before, I finally began. The glue didn't dry. The sand kept falling through. On the day, water dripped all over the table while the judges watched.
If I had begun early, the leaks would have shown themselves at home, where nobody was watching. I delayed so I wouldn't look weak, and that's exactly how I looked."

qa.q: What model did young Irawati want to build?
qa.a: She wanted to build a water filter.

qa.q: Why did young Irawati keep saying "Tomorrow"?
qa.a: She felt frightened that a leaking model would show everyone she wasn't clever, so putting it off felt safer than starting badly.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have changed the outcome?
qa.a: Starting early would have let the leaks show up at home, where she could fix them without anyone watching.

qa.q: How might Irawati's mother have seen those evenings of "Tomorrow"?
qa.a: Her mother may have thought she was just lazy or busy, not knowing the fear of being judged was behind it.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a teenager who put off a project because a poor result would reveal weakness, which made the final work worse.

passage:
Vasudha's science-fair project on seed germination was due on Friday, and she had known about it for a month. Every evening she opened the folder, looked at the blank title page and closed it. If it turned out badly, everyone in Class 10 would see it on the board, with her name in big letters.
On Wednesday night she finally started. Then the power went off across the street, the inverter beeped and died, and the laptop she shared with her brother Yusuf had eleven percent battery. The seeds she had soaked were only a day old, not two weeks.
By candlelight, she drew sprouts she had never grown and wrote a conclusion she could not prove.
Yusuf, reading his comic with a torch, said, "Why didn't you start last month?"
Vasudha didn't answer. The honest reason was that starting would have meant being judged sooner.

qa.q: How much battery did the shared laptop have when the power went off?
qa.a: It had eleven percent battery.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha keep closing the folder for a month?
qa.a: She felt anxious that a bad result would be seen by the whole class with her name on it, so delaying protected her from being judged.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Vasudha try next time?
qa.a: Delaying left no time for the seeds to grow and no margin for the power cut; next time she could start with one small step early, like soaking the seeds, before worrying about the result.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see Vasudha's situation?
qa.a: Yusuf sees it simply as poor timing and asks why she didn't start earlier, not knowing the fear of judgement behind the delay.

grounding: It shows a teenager putting off a project because a poor result would expose her, which protects her self-image but makes the final work worse.

passage:
Ganga's school film club was screening every Class 11 short film in the auditorium, with parents invited. Her script had been ready in her head for weeks. Her camera, borrowed from her aunt, sat in its case.
"When are we shooting?" her friend Yamini asked on Monday. "I'm free all week to act."
"Soon. I'm still thinking."
She kept thinking. Thinking was safe. Nobody could call a film in your head clumsy.
On the Sunday before the screening, she finally called Yamini. They shot everything in one afternoon, in bad light, with the neighbour's pressure cooker whistling through every scene. There was no time to reshoot.
In the auditorium, the audience laughed at the wrong places. Ganga sank low in her seat. The film everyone saw really was clumsy, just as she had feared.

qa.q: When did Ganga finally call Yamini to shoot?
qa.a: Ganga called Yamini on the Sunday before the screening.

qa.q: Why did Ganga keep saying she was still thinking?
qa.a: She felt afraid that a real film would be judged as clumsy, while a film in her head could not fail, so delaying felt safe.

qa.q: What could Ganga have done differently?
qa.a: She could have shot a rough first version early in the week with Yamini, so there was time to fix the light and sound before anyone saw it.

qa.q: What is it like for Yamini to wait all week?
qa.a: Yamini, who was free to act all week, may feel frustrated and let down to end up rushing through one afternoon in bad light.

grounding: It shows a teenager delaying her film because a poor result might reveal weakness, which protects her self-image but makes the final film worse.

qa.q: Why does Chaitanya keep delaying the model?
qa.a: Chaitanya is afraid a real attempt will turn out bad and show everyone Chaitanya isn't as good as Rhea or Sunil; a last-night rush offers an excuse, which feels safer.

qa.q: What makes Sumit's offer a good next step?

qa.q: How does Sumit see the delay?
qa.a: Sumit sees plainly that the last-night plan will make the model worse, and is a bit exasperated but still wants to help.
